article.headline: REZE Studio Brings Professional MMD Animation Editing to the Browser
article.lede: When the official Three.js account spotlighted REZE Studio this April, it pointed — with a mild irony — to a tool built not on Three.js but on a hand-rolled WebGPU renderer. REZE Studio is a browser-native, professional-grade animation curve editor for the MMD ecosystem: the vast world of free 3D models and motion files that anime fan-animators have shared since 2008. It is the most serious attempt yet to replace MikuMikuDance, a Windows-only application whose development effectively concluded in 2019.
article.body:
The screenshot that earned the Three.js account's attention tells the technical story in miniature. A skeleton with **147 bones** — including 22 in each hand for full finger articulation — plays a motion clip called `miku.vmd` at 60 frames per second across 2,889 frames, roughly 48 seconds of animation. The file name is a marker of provenance: *VMD*, or Vocaloid Motion Data, is the binary format native to *MikuMikuDance* (MMD), a free animation tool released in 2008 by Japanese developer Yu Higuchi specifically to animate Hatsune Miku, the virtual idol released by Crypton Future Media the year before. VMD files encode bone keyframes — position, rotation quaternion, and 64 bytes of Bézier interpolation parameters per keyframe — in a format that bakes in Shift-JIS Japanese character encoding, a relic of its desktop-software origins. The v0.10 label in the screenshot refers to the rendering engine's version, not the application's.

What the screenshot does not show is equally significant. *MikuMikuDance* itself is Windows-only freeware whose meaningful development concluded with version 7.39 in 2011, with sporadic updates through 2019. In the interim, tens of thousands of creators built a sharing economy around *PMX* skeleton models and VMD motion files, distributed freely on Niconico and YouTube. That content library has outlived the tool. Animators wanting professional control have been migrating to Blender via a community *mmd_tools* addon — an upgrade that imports both skill-curve and software complexity that the original MMD community never had to pay.

REZE Studio, built by AmyangXYZ — a computer science doctoral candidate at the University of Connecticut — runs directly in the browser, on desktops and iPads alike, with no installation. It loads PMX skeleton files, imports and exports VMD animations, and offers a professional timeline with a *dopesheet*, per-channel Bézier curve editing, a 3D transform gizmo, and animation layers with blend weights. The GPLv3 license makes it open-source; the GitHub repository has 356 stars and active commit history as of early May 2026.

The rendering layer — *reze-engine* — bypasses Three.js entirely and writes directly to the WebGPU API, the next-generation browser graphics specification now production-ready across Chrome, Firefox, and Safari as of late 2025. Amyang hand-wrote the physics solver (roughly 1,500 lines of sequential-impulse rigid-body simulation), offloaded bone matrix computation to GPU compute shaders to handle models with 400-plus bones, and implemented a VMD serializer that preserves the Shift-JIS bone-name encoding that legacy files depend on. The visual output favors a recognizable anime aesthetic: toon shading, rim lighting, screen-space outlines, and an 'alpha-hashed' transparency pass for overlapping geometry.

The broader direction is visible in Amyang's companion tools. MiKaPo converts webcam or video input into VMD motion data in real time using pose estimation, allowing animators to bootstrap keyframe animation from footage and refine it in REZE Studio. Together the projects constitute a web-native reimagining of a creative pipeline the MMD community has sustained on Windows desktops for almost two decades. The open *VRM* avatar standard — built on glTF 2.0 and favored by the VTuber and virtual-avatar industry — likely represents the next step, superseding binary VMD with browser-friendly, standardized animation files. REZE Studio bridges both worlds: it speaks VMD today, and its WebGPU foundation is positioned for whatever the open web settles on next.

concepts.definition: Freeware 3D animation software released in 2008 by Japanese developer Yu Higuchi, originally designed to animate the virtual idol Hatsune Miku. It became the foundation of an enormous anime fan-animation ecosystem built around freely shared models and motion files. Development effectively concluded in 2019; it runs only on Windows.

The binary animation file format native to MikuMikuDance. It stores bone keyframes — position, rotation quaternion, and Bézier interpolation parameters — along with morph and camera keyframes, with bone names encoded in Shift-JIS Japanese text. VMD files are freely shared throughout the MMD creator community.

A next-generation browser graphics API that gives JavaScript direct access to GPU hardware for rendering and compute workloads, succeeding WebGL. It reached production readiness across major browsers in late 2025 and enables significantly more complex and efficient 3D rendering than its predecessor.

The current skeleton-and-mesh model format used in MikuMikuDance. A PMX file contains the 3D mesh, bone hierarchy, physics rig, and material definitions for an animated character. Community-created PMX models are freely distributed across Niconico and YouTube.

A technique in skeletal animation where the position of an end point — such as a hand or foot — drives the rotation of the bones above it in the hierarchy, rather than animating each joint independently. Critical for convincing character animation, particularly for foot contact with surfaces.

A view in professional animation software that displays all keyframes for all animation channels on a shared timeline, allowing animators to see and adjust the timing of motion across bones simultaneously. The term is borrowed from traditional hand-drawn animation workflows.

An open file format for humanoid 3D avatars built on the glTF 2.0 standard, maintained by the VRM Consortium and favored by the VTuber and virtual-avatar industry. It is a browser-friendly, standardized alternative to proprietary formats like PMX, with a companion animation format called VRMA.

A method of smoothing animation between keyframes using cubic Bézier curves to control the rate of change over time — how fast or slow a bone accelerates and decelerates between two poses. It offers finer creative control than linear interpolation and is the standard in professional animation tools.

A character encoding for the Japanese writing system common in legacy Windows software. VMD files use Shift-JIS to encode bone names, a format detail that any modern tool must handle explicitly to remain compatible with the existing archive of community-created MMD content.

A community-developed Blender add-on that imports and exports PMX model files and VMD animation data, allowing animators to work with the MMD content library inside Blender. It became the primary migration path for creators who outgrew MikuMikuDance's native toolset.

A method of simulating physics constraints — collisions, joints, cloth — by iteratively resolving collision impulses across many small time steps. Common in real-time physics engines; REZE Studio's implementation runs at a fixed 60Hz timestep with up to six substeps per frame.

repos.summary: The source code for REZE Studio, a browser-native MMD animation curve editor. Built with Next.js, React, and TypeScript, it handles PMX model loading, VMD import and export, professional timeline editing with a dopesheet, and real-time 3D viewport interaction. Licensed GPLv3 and actively maintained.

A custom WebGPU renderer in TypeScript that powers REZE Studio and its companion tools. Written with near-zero external dependencies, it implements toon and Blinn-Phong shading, a hand-written sequential-impulse physics solver, GPU compute shaders for bone matrix calculation, and a full VMD/PMX pipeline including Shift-JIS encoding support. Available as an npm package.

A companion tool by the same developer that converts real-time webcam or video input into VMD motion data using pose estimation. Allows animators to bootstrap keyframe animation from footage, which can then be refined inside REZE Studio. Had accumulated 581 stars as of early May 2026.

article.fact_check: The tweet was posted by the official @threejs account, but REZE Studio is not built on Three.js. Its rendering engine (reze-engine) writes directly to the WebGPU API without using the Three.js scene graph abstraction. The @threejs account regularly highlights interesting web 3D work that extends beyond its own library.
